questions.title: What distinguishes a threat from persecution in asylum cases?
questions.question_body: In the opinion, the court says that threats alone are insufficient to establish past persecution. I’ve read that asylum requires ‘more than mere restrictions or threats to life and liberty’, but I’m unclear on how the courts determine what level of harm crosses that threshold. What factors are considered when evaluating whether a threat, or a series of threats, constitute persecution?

questions.title: How does the ‘central reason’ test apply to political-opinion persecution?
questions.question_body: Petitioners allege that they were targeted because of their political opinion, yet the court found that the violence was primarily motivated by Jimenez’s conflict with Don Rafa. The court refers to the ‘central reason’ test from Rivera‑Barrientos and Dallakoti. Could someone explain how the central‑reason test is applied when a persecutor has multiple motives, and what evidence is necessary to satisfy that one protected ground is a central reason?

questions.title: What is the standard of review for the BIA’s findings of fact under § 1252(b)(4)(A)?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that the court reviews the BIA’s findings of fact under a substantial‑evidence standard. I’ve seen the term used in other contexts, but can anyone clarify what “substantial evidence” means in this particular review, and how it differs from the standard used in merits‑review decisions by immigration judges?

questions.title: Why did the court refuse to consider the petitioners’ fear of future persecution under the ‘unable or unwilling’ test?
questions.question_body: The opinion disclaims that the petitioners failed to show that the Colombian government was unwilling or unable to protect them, citing insufficient reporting. How does the ‘unable or unwilling’ analysis weigh evidence of the government’s response to past persecution, and why is a lack of police reporting not fatal in other cases?

questions.title: What does ‘safe internal relocation’ mean in asylum law, and why did the court reject the petitioners’ claims?
questions.question_body: The opinion dismisses the petitioners’ argument that they cannot safely relocate within Colombia, citing that they lived safely with relatives for three weeks. How is ‘safe internal relocation’ evaluated, what evidence is required, and why did the court find relocation to be ‘reasonable’ despite the petitioners’ claims of insecurity?

questions.title: How are asylum and withholding of removal interrelated in terms of the burden of proof?
questions.question_body: The court notes that if a petitioner fails to meet asylum criteria, they also fail to meet the higher standard for withholding of removal. Could someone walk me through the logic linking these two reliefs, especially the preponderance of evidence burden for asylum vs. the well‑founded fear standard for withholding?

questions.title: What role does a provisional law license play in asylum proceedings?
questions.question_body: Jimenez is described as a provisional lawyer who investigated a property dispute. He claims his role might have made him a target. Does having legal credentials or the perception of being a law‑student influence an asylum applicant’s credibility or affect how the court analyzes persecution rooted in professional activities?
